lessons.title: The Board & The Pawn
learningOutcomes: **Name** all 64 squares on a chessboard using algebraic notation.
**Move** a Pawn correctly — one square forward, two on first move, diagonal capture.
**Value** patience and foundation — understanding that every grandmaster started by learning the board one square at a time.
lessons.inquiryQuestion: How does the Pawn move forward one step at a time — and how can we use the same patience to build our chess skills step by step?

lessons.title: The Rook
learningOutcomes: **Move** a Rook correctly along ranks and files.
**Calculate** how many squares a Rook controls from any given position.
**Value** directness — understanding that sometimes the straight path is the most powerful.
lessons.inquiryQuestion: How does the Rook charge straight down a corridor — and when is the direct path more powerful than the clever one?

lessons.title: The Bishop
learningOutcomes: **Move** a Bishop correctly along diagonals.
**Identify** which color squares each bishop controls and why bishops are stuck on one color.
**Value** specialized vision — understanding that seeing from a unique angle is a strength, not a weakness.
lessons.inquiryQuestion: How does the Bishop see the board from its diagonal angle — and why is being 'stuck' on one color actually a strength?

lessons.title: The Queen
learningOutcomes: **Move** the Queen correctly — combining Rook and Bishop powers.
**Compare** the Queen's movement to Rook + Bishop and understand why it is worth 9 points.
**Value** versatility — understanding that combining skills makes you more powerful than any single skill alone.
lessons.inquiryQuestion: How did the Queen become the most powerful piece on the board — and what happens when you combine two strengths into one?

lessons.title: The King
learningOutcomes: **Move** the King correctly — one square in any direction.
**Explain** why the King is the most important piece even though it moves slowly.
**Value** protection — understanding that the most valuable things often need the most care.
lessons.inquiryQuestion: Why is the slowest-moving piece also the most important — and what does that teach us about leadership?

lessons.title: The Knight
learningOutcomes: **Move** the Knight correctly in an L-shape.
**Identify** why the Knight is the only piece that can jump over others.
**Value** creative movement — understanding that doing things differently is not wrong, it's a superpower.
lessons.inquiryQuestion: How does the Knight's weird L-shaped jump make it the most creative piece — and when is being different an advantage?

lessons.title: Special Moves: Castling
learningOutcomes: **Execute** castling correctly — king-side and queen-side.
**Identify** all conditions that make castling illegal.
**Value** teamwork — understanding that the King and Rook protect each other by working together.
lessons.inquiryQuestion: How do the King and Rook team up to keep the King safe — and when is the best time to castle?

lessons.title: Special Moves: En Passant & Promotion
learningOutcomes: **Execute** en passant correctly.
**Explain** pawn promotion and why the Queen is almost always the best choice.
**Value** perseverance — understanding that even the weakest piece can become the strongest.
lessons.inquiryQuestion: How can the weakest piece on the board become the strongest — and what does that teach us about never giving up?

lessons.title: Check & Checkmate
learningOutcomes: **Distinguish** between check, checkmate, and stalemate.
**Identify** three ways to escape check: move the King, block the check, capture the attacker.
**Value** awareness — understanding that threats must be seen before they can be stopped.
lessons.inquiryQuestion: What is the difference between a warning and a knockout — and how do you know when the game is truly over?

lessons.title: Stalemate & Draws
learningOutcomes: **Identify** stalemate, insufficient material, threefold repetition, and the 50-move rule.
**Evaluate** when a draw is a good result versus when it is a missed opportunity.
**Value** resourcefulness — understanding that a draw is not a failure but a skillful escape.
lessons.inquiryQuestion: How can a game with no winner still be a triumph — and when is escaping with a draw the smartest move?

lessons.title: Forks
learningOutcomes: **Identify** a fork in a given position.
**Create** a fork using the Knight, Pawn, or Queen.
**Value** efficiency — understanding that one move that does two things is better than two moves that do one.
lessons.inquiryQuestion: How can one Knight attack two targets at once — and what makes a fork the Knight's signature weapon?

lessons.title: Pins
learningOutcomes: **Identify** absolute and relative pins.
**Explain** why a pinned piece cannot move without exposing a more valuable piece.
**Value** restraint — understanding that holding something in place can be as powerful as capturing it.
lessons.inquiryQuestion: How does the Bishop hold an enemy piece hostage along a diagonal — and why can't the pinned piece simply walk away?

lessons.title: Skewers
learningOutcomes: **Distinguish** between a pin and a skewer.
**Create** a skewer along a rank, file, or diagonal.
**Value** reversal — understanding that flipping a pattern (pin → skewer) creates a new weapon.
lessons.inquiryQuestion: What happens when you flip a pin upside down — and how does the Rook's straight line become an X-ray weapon?

lessons.title: Discovered Attacks
learningOutcomes: **Identify** when moving one piece reveals an attack from another.
**Create** a discovered check by moving a blocking piece.
**Value** coordination — understanding that the power of one piece depends on the position of another.
lessons.inquiryQuestion: How does moving one piece suddenly unleash the power of another — and why is the discovered attack chess's best surprise?

lessons.title: Removing the Defender
learningOutcomes: **Identify** when a piece is defended by another and how to remove that defense.
**Calculate** trades where you capture the defender to win the defended piece.
**Value** persistence — understanding that attacking the guard is often easier than attacking the target.
lessons.inquiryQuestion: How do you capture a piece that is protected — and why is attacking the guard sometimes smarter than attacking the treasure?

lessons.title: Deflection
learningOutcomes: **Identify** when a piece is overworked — defending two things at once.
**Create** a deflection by attacking one defended target to force the defender away.
**Value** precision — understanding that forcing the opponent to choose between two defenses creates an opening.
lessons.inquiryQuestion: How do you make a piece choose between protecting two friends — and what happens when it can only save one?

lessons.title: Decoys & Sacrifices
learningOutcomes: **Identify** when sacrificing a piece will lure the opponent into a trap.
**Calculate** a sacrifice that forces the King into a mating net.
**Value** courage — understanding that giving up material for a greater goal is the mark of a strong player.
lessons.inquiryQuestion: When is giving away your most powerful piece the smartest move — and how do you know the sacrifice will pay off?

lessons.title: Back-rank Mates
learningOutcomes: **Identify** when a King is trapped on the back rank with no escape squares.
**Create** a back-rank mate using Rook or Queen.
**Value** awareness — understanding that the edge of the board can be a prison, not a wall.
lessons.inquiryQuestion: Why is the first row the most dangerous place for a King — and how does the Rook turn a corridor into a trap?

lessons.title: Mate in 1 Patterns
learningOutcomes: **Recognize** common mate-in-1 patterns: back rank, smothered, corner, corridor.
**Deliver** checkmate in one move from a given position.
**Value** finishing — understanding that recognizing the end is as important as playing the beginning.
lessons.inquiryQuestion: How do you know when one move will end the game — and what patterns should you train your eyes to see instantly?

lessons.title: Mate in 2 Introduction
learningOutcomes: **Calculate** a forced mate in two moves.
**Explain** the concept of a 'forcing move' — check, capture, or threat.
**Value** foresight — understanding that the best players see the future before it happens.
lessons.inquiryQuestion: How do you force your opponent into a mate they cannot escape — and what is the difference between a threat and a forced win?

lessons.title: Opening Principles
learningOutcomes: **Apply** the three opening principles: control the center, develop pieces, castle early.
**Evaluate** opening moves as good, okay, or bad based on these principles.
**Value** preparation — understanding that the opening sets the stage for everything that follows.
lessons.inquiryQuestion: How do the first ten moves set the stage for the entire game — and why is controlling the center like building a house on solid ground?

lessons.title: The Italian Game & Spanish Game
learningOutcomes: **Play** the first 5-6 moves of the Italian Game (1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6 3.Bc4) and Spanish (3.Bb5).
**Explain** why these openings develop pieces toward the center.
**Value** tradition — understanding that classic patterns have lasted centuries for a reason.
lessons.inquiryQuestion: Why have the Italian and Spanish openings been played for 500 years — and what makes a classic opening stand the test of time?

lessons.title: The Sicilian Defense
learningOutcomes: **Play** the first 5-6 moves of the Sicilian Defense (1.e4 c5).
**Explain** why Black gives up center control to fight for it later.
**Value** counter-punching — understanding that you don't always need to mirror your opponent's plan.
lessons.inquiryQuestion: Why does Black let White control the center first — and how does fighting for it later create a sharper, more exciting game?

lessons.title: Pawn Structures
learningOutcomes: **Identify** pawn chains, pawn islands, and passed pawns.
**Evaluate** which side has the better pawn structure.
**Value** structure — understanding that pawns are the bones of a position; everything else hangs on them.
lessons.inquiryQuestion: Why do grandmasters say pawns are the soul of chess — and how do these little pieces shape the entire battlefield?

lessons.title: Piece Activity & Outposts
learningOutcomes: **Identify** an outpost — a square in enemy territory protected by a pawn and unreachable by enemy pawns.
**Place** pieces on their most active squares.
**Value** positioning — understanding that where a piece stands is more important than what it threatens.
lessons.inquiryQuestion: What makes a square 'strong' — and why is a Knight on an outpost worth more than a Knight in the corner?

lessons.title: Space & Initiative
learningOutcomes: **Evaluate** which side controls more space.
**Explain** the difference between having space and using it effectively.
**Value** aggression — understanding that controlling more squares forces the opponent into a defensive shell.
lessons.inquiryQuestion: How does controlling more of the board force your opponent to shrink — and why is having space useless if you don't use it?

lessons.title: Weaknesses: Doubled, Isolated, Backward Pawns
learningOutcomes: **Identify** doubled, isolated, and backward pawns.
**Explain** why these pawn weaknesses are targets for the opponent.
**Value** solidity — understanding that a solid structure withstands pressure better than a flashy one.
lessons.inquiryQuestion: Why are some pawns weak just because of who their neighbors are — and how do you turn your opponent's structural flaws into your targets?

lessons.title: The Bishop Pair
learningOutcomes: **Explain** why two bishops together are more valuable than bishop + knight.
**Identify** when preserving the bishop pair is worth avoiding trades.
**Value** synergy — understanding that two pieces working together are stronger than the sum of their parts.
lessons.inquiryQuestion: Why are two Bishops worth more than Bishop + Knight — and what makes them the ultimate long-range team?

lessons.title: Good vs Bad Bishops
learningOutcomes: **Distinguish** between a good bishop (active, outside pawn chain) and a bad bishop (blocked by own pawns).
**Evaluate** when to trade a bad bishop for a knight.
**Value** honesty — understanding that admitting a piece is bad and trading it is smarter than pretending it's fine.
lessons.inquiryQuestion: How can the same piece be a hero in one position and a prisoner in another — and when is trading your 'bad' bishop the smartest move?

lessons.title: Planning in the Middlegame
learningOutcomes: **Create** a plan from a middlegame position: identify weaknesses, find targets, choose an attack or improvement.
**Explain** the difference between having a plan and making random moves.
**Value** strategy — understanding that a mediocre plan is better than no plan at all.
lessons.inquiryQuestion: How do you create a plan when there are no obvious captures — and why is a bad plan better than no plan?

lessons.title: Calculation Technique
learningOutcomes: **Apply** the calculation method: candidate moves → forcing lines → evaluation.
**Calculate** 2-3 moves ahead consistently.
**Value** discipline — understanding that calculation is a muscle that strengthens with practice.
lessons.inquiryQuestion: How do grandmasters see five moves ahead — and what technique lets you calculate deeper without getting lost?

lessons.title: Advanced Tactics: Zwischenzug
learningOutcomes: **Identify** when an intermediate move (zwischenzug) is stronger than the expected recapture.
**Create** a zwischenzug that changes the evaluation of a sequence.
**Value** surprise — understanding that the obvious move is not always the best move.
lessons.inquiryQuestion: What happens when you play a surprising move in the middle of an expected sequence — and why is the 'in-between' move often the strongest?

lessons.title: Advanced Tactics: Desperado
learningOutcomes: **Identify** when a doomed piece can capture something on its way out.
**Calculate** a desperado sequence that minimizes losses.
**Value** resilience — understanding that even a losing piece can fight back before it falls.
lessons.inquiryQuestion: What can a doomed piece do before it falls — and how do you make your last move count?

lessons.title: Rook Endgames
learningOutcomes: **Play** the Lucena position (winning) and Philidor position (drawing) correctly.
**Explain** why rook + pawn vs rook is the most common endgame and must be learned.
**Value** precision — understanding that endgames are unforgiving and one mistake ruins everything.
lessons.inquiryQuestion: Why do even grandmasters struggle with Rook endgames — and what makes the Lucena and Philidor positions essential?

lessons.title: Pawn Endgames
learningOutcomes: **Apply** opposition, triangulation, and the square rule in pawn endgames.
**Evaluate** whether a pawn will queen before the enemy King can stop it.
**Value** purity — understanding that pawn endgames teach you how pieces truly move because there are no tricks, only truth.
lessons.inquiryQuestion: How can two Kings and a few pawns contain more depth than a board full of pieces — and why is the opposition the most important concept in chess?

lessons.title: Minor Piece Endgames
learningOutcomes: **Evaluate** whether bishop or knight is stronger in a given endgame.
**Explain** why same-color bishop endgames are often draws.
**Value** nuance — understanding that the same pieces behave differently when most other pieces are gone.
lessons.inquiryQuestion: Why is a Bishop sometimes a hero and sometimes a prisoner in the endgame — and how do you know which one you have?

lessons.title: Attacking the Castled King
learningOutcomes: **Identify** when the kingside pawn shield is weak enough to attack.
**Create** an attack using sacrifices to open lines toward the King.
**Value** courage — understanding that attacking the enemy King requires both calculation and bravery.
lessons.inquiryQuestion: How do you break through the wall of pawns protecting the King — and when is the right moment to sacrifice for a mating attack?

lessons.title: Counterplay & Defense
learningOutcomes: **Identify** counter-attacking resources in a defensive position.
**Apply** prophylaxis — preventing the opponent's threats before they happen.
**Value** defense — understanding that great attackers are also great defenders.
lessons.inquiryQuestion: How do you defend when your opponent has the initiative — and why is the best defense often a counter-attack?

lessons.title: Positional Sacrifices
learningOutcomes: **Evaluate** when a sacrifice of material gives lasting positional compensation.
**Identify** common positional sacrifices: exchange sacrifice, pawn sacrifices for initiative.
**Value** investment — understanding that giving up something now for something better later is a life skill.
lessons.inquiryQuestion: When is giving away your Queen (or Rook) for nothing immediate the best move — and how do you judge 'compensation'?

lessons.title: Transition to Endgame
learningOutcomes: **Evaluate** when trading pieces helps you reach a winning endgame.
**Identify** which pieces to trade and which to keep.
**Value** transition — understanding that knowing when to switch from middlegame to endgame is a master skill.
lessons.inquiryQuestion: How do you know when to stop attacking and start trading — and why is the transition to endgame the hardest phase to judge?

lessons.title: Advanced Opening Theory
learningOutcomes: **Navigate** 10+ moves deep in a chosen opening.
**Explain** the strategic ideas behind opening moves, not just memorizing them.
**Value** preparation — understanding that tournament success comes from homework, not just talent.
lessons.inquiryQuestion: How do grandmasters memorize thousands of opening moves — and what is the difference between knowing a move and understanding it?

lessons.title: Prophylactic Thinking
learningOutcomes: **Identify** the opponent's plan before they execute it.
**Create** moves that prevent the opponent's threats rather than just reacting to them.
**Value** prevention — understanding that stopping a problem before it starts is better than solving it after.
lessons.inquiryQuestion: How do you know what your opponent wants before they do it — and why is preventing their plan more powerful than reacting to it?

lessons.title: The Initiative vs Material
learningOutcomes: **Evaluate** whether initiative (attack) or material (points) is more important in a given position.
**Explain** the concept of 'compensation' for sacrificed material.
**Value** judgment — understanding that chess has no formula; every decision is a judgment call.
lessons.inquiryQuestion: When is attacking worth more than having extra pieces — and how do you judge when to trade material for initiative?

lessons.title: Time Trouble & Practical Play
learningOutcomes: **Manage** time in a game: when to think, when to play quickly.
**Apply** practical decision-making when low on time.
**Value** composure — understanding that panic is the enemy in time trouble.
lessons.inquiryQuestion: How do great players think clearly when the clock is ticking down — and what separates calm intuition from panic?

lessons.title: Analysis & Self-Review
learningOutcomes: **Analyze** your own games to find mistakes and missed opportunities.
**Use** an engine to check analysis without becoming dependent on it.
**Value** honesty — understanding that the only way to improve is to admit your mistakes.
lessons.inquiryQuestion: How do you learn more from your losses than your wins — and why is engine analysis a tool, not a crutch?

lessons.title: Teaching Chess to Others
learningOutcomes: **Explain** a chess concept clearly to a beginner.
**Adapt** your explanation to the learner's level and learning style.
**Value** teaching — understanding that teaching is the final test of mastery.
lessons.inquiryQuestion: How do you explain something you know deeply to someone who knows nothing — and why is teaching the truest test of understanding?

lessons.title: Creating Studies & Puzzles
learningOutcomes: **Compose** an original chess puzzle with a clear tactical theme.
**Validate** that your puzzle has exactly one solution.
**Value** creativity — understanding that creating puzzles deepens understanding more than solving them.
lessons.inquiryQuestion: How do you create a puzzle that is challenging but fair — and why is composing harder than solving?

lessons.title: Blindfold Chess
learningOutcomes: **Visualize** a chess position without looking at the board.
**Play** 5-10 moves blindfolded with increasing accuracy.
**Value** imagination — understanding that the board exists in your mind, not just on the table.
lessons.inquiryQuestion: How do grandmasters play entire games without seeing the board — and what does blindfold chess teach us about mental visualization?

lessons.title: Chess Psychology
learningOutcomes: **Identify** signs of tilt, overconfidence, and time panic in yourself and opponents.
**Apply** techniques to stay calm under pressure: breathing, routines, positive self-talk.
**Value** sportsmanship — understanding that how you win and lose defines you more than your rating.
lessons.inquiryQuestion: Why do even the best players make terrible moves when they're upset — and how do you master your own mind before you master the board?

lessons.title: Your Chess Journey
learningOutcomes: **Set** realistic chess goals: rating targets, tournament plans, study routines.
**Create** a personal study plan combining tactics, openings, endgames, and games analysis.
**Value** the journey — understanding that chess is not a destination but a lifelong path of improvement.
lessons.inquiryQuestion: Where will chess take you next — and how do you keep improving when there is no final level to beat?

lessons.title: The King's Pawn Opening
learningOutcomes: **Play** the first 5 moves of a 1.e4 e5 opening correctly.
**Explain** why both sides fight for the center with pawns.
**Value** tradition — understanding that this is how chess has been played for centuries.
lessons.inquiryQuestion: Why has 1.e4 e5 been the most common first move pair for 500 years — and what does this simple pawn move unlock?

lessons.title: The Italian Game
learningOutcomes: **Play** the Italian Game through move 6 for both sides.
**Explain** why 3.Bc4 targets f7 and helps development.
**Value** clarity — understanding that simple, natural moves can be profoundly strong.
lessons.inquiryQuestion: How does the Italian Game teach us that the simplest development is often the best — and why has it been played for centuries?

lessons.title: The Evans Gambit
learningOutcomes: **Play** the Evans Gambit accepted and declined.
**Calculate** the compensation White gets for the sacrificed pawn.
**Value** courage — understanding that giving up a pawn for rapid development is a valid strategy.
lessons.inquiryQuestion: Why would White give away a pawn on move 4 — and how does the Evans Gambit turn opening theory into an adventure?

lessons.title: The Two Knights Defense
learningOutcomes: **Play** the Two Knights Defense through move 8.
**Identify** the key tactical motifs in the Traxler and Fried Liver lines.
**Value** boldness — understanding that defending actively can be more powerful than passive defense.
lessons.inquiryQuestion: How does Black's second knight turn a calm Italian Game into a tactical battlefield — and who benefits from the chaos?

lessons.title: The Fried Liver Attack
learningOutcomes: **Execute** the Fried Liver Attack against the Two Knights Defense.
**Defend** against the Fried Liver using the Traxler or Na5.
**Value** calculation — understanding that sharp attacks require precise defense.
lessons.inquiryQuestion: Is the Fried Liver Attack a brilliant trap or a reckless gamble — and how do you survive it as Black?

lessons.title: The Ruy Lopez (Spanish)
learningOutcomes: **Play** the Ruy Lopez Exchange and Closed variations through move 8.
**Explain** why 3.Bb5 is more subtle than 3.Bc4.
**Value** patience — understanding that the Spanish takes time to unfold but rewards deep study.
lessons.inquiryQuestion: Why is the Ruy Lopez called 'the Spanish Torture' — and how does a simple bishop move on move 3 create decades of theory?

lessons.title: The Scotch Game
learningOutcomes: **Play** the Scotch Game main lines through move 8.
**Compare** the Scotch to the Italian and Ruy Lopez.
**Value** directness — understanding that opening the center early has both risks and rewards.
lessons.inquiryQuestion: How does the Scotch Game blast open the center on move 3 — and when is direct aggression better than quiet buildup?

lessons.title: The Petroff Defense
learningOutcomes: **Play** the Petroff main line through move 8.
**Explain** why Black mirrors White's move and what they hope to achieve.
**Value** solidity — understanding that not every opening needs to be sharp to be strong.
lessons.inquiryQuestion: How does Black copying White's move 2 create one of the most solid defenses in chess — and why do aggressive players hate facing it?

lessons.title: The Vienna Game
learningOutcomes: **Play** the Vienna Game through move 6.
**Explain** the difference between the Vienna and the Italian.
**Value** flexibility — understanding that delaying Nf3 keeps options open.
lessons.inquiryQuestion: What happens when White waits to develop the knight to f3 — and how does the Vienna Game hide its teeth?

lessons.title: The Ponziani Opening
learningOutcomes: **Play** the Ponziani Opening through move 8.
**Explain** the ideas behind 3.c3 and the d4 break.
**Value** exploration — understanding that unpopular openings can be effective surprises.
lessons.inquiryQuestion: Why did the Ponziani disappear from top-level chess — and why might it be the perfect surprise weapon for you?

lessons.title: Sicilian Defense: Introduction
learningOutcomes: **Explain** why 1...c5 is the most popular reply to 1.e4.
**Identify** the strategic themes of the Sicilian: pawn break ...d5, semi-open c-file, queenside counterplay.
**Value** fighting spirit — understanding that Black can play for a win from move 1.
lessons.inquiryQuestion: Why does Black give up the center on move 1 — and how does the Sicilian turn defense into a counter-attack?

lessons.title: Sicilian: Najdorf Variation
learningOutcomes: **Play** the Najdorf through move 10 for both sides.
**Explain** the significance of ...a6 and the English Attack (Be3, f3, Qd2, O-O-O).
**Value** depth — understanding that the Najdorf is chess's deepest opening ocean.
lessons.inquiryQuestion: Why has the Najdorf been the battleground for world champions for 70 years — and what makes 5...a6 so important?

lessons.title: Sicilian: Dragon Variation
learningOutcomes: **Play** the Dragon through move 10.
**Identify** the Yugoslav Attack (Be3, f3, Qd2, O-O-O) and Black's counterplay on the c-file.
**Value** bravery — understanding that castling on opposite sides means both players are racing to attack.
lessons.inquiryQuestion: How does the Dragon's fianchettoed bishop turn the Sicilian into a race of opposite-side attacks — and who reaches the king first?

lessons.title: Sicilian: Scheveningen
learningOutcomes: **Play** the Scheveningen through move 10.
**Explain** the ...e6/...d6 pawn chain and the central breaks ...e5 and ...d5.
**Value** flexibility — understanding that keeping options open is a strength.
lessons.inquiryQuestion: How does the Scheveningen's flexible center let Black choose their plan — and why is flexibility sometimes sharper than aggression?

lessons.title: Sicilian: Taimanov Variation
learningOutcomes: **Play** the Taimanov through move 10.
**Explain** Black's plan of ...Nge7, ...a6, and ...Qc7.
**Value** subtlety — understanding that quiet development can hide dangerous intentions.
lessons.inquiryQuestion: How does the Taimanov's quiet knight development set up a flexible middlegame — and why is it a favorite of modern grandmasters?

lessons.title: Sicilian: Kan (Paulsen)
learningOutcomes: **Play** the Kan through move 10.
**Explain** the ...a6/...b5 queenside expansion plan.
**Value** patience — understanding that waiting for the right moment to strike is a valid strategy.
lessons.inquiryQuestion: How does the Kan's patient ...a6 prepare a long-term queenside attack — and when does patience turn to power?

lessons.title: Sicilian: Classical Variation
learningOutcomes: **Play** the Classical Sicilian through move 10.
**Explain** the differences between Classical and Najdorf/Dragon.
**Value** tradition — understanding that older lines are still playable at all levels.
lessons.inquiryQuestion: What happened to the Classical Sicilian after the Najdorf took over — and why is it still a reliable choice?

lessons.title: Sicilian: Alapin (2.c3)
learningOutcomes: **Play** the Alapin through move 8.
**Explain** why White avoids the main-line Open Sicilian.
**Value** pragmatism — understanding that sidestepping theory is a legitimate strategy.
lessons.inquiryQuestion: How does 2.c3 avoid the Sicilian jungle — and why do some players prefer a quiet life over theoretical warfare?

lessons.title: Sicilian: Closed (2.Nc3)
learningOutcomes: **Play** the Closed Sicilian through move 8.
**Explain** the kingside buildup with g3, Bg2, f4.
**Value** restraint — understanding that not every position needs to be opened immediately.
lessons.inquiryQuestion: How does the Closed Sicilian build an attack without opening the center — and when does quiet become deadly?

lessons.title: Sicilian: Grand Prix Attack
learningOutcomes: **Play** the Grand Prix Attack through move 8.
**Explain** the kingside pawn storm with f4, Nf3, Bc4.
**Value** aggression — understanding that a direct pawn storm on the kingside can outweigh queenside counterplay.
lessons.inquiryQuestion: How does the Grand Prix Attack's pawn storm challenge the Sicilian's queenside counterplay — and who wins the race?

lessons.title: French Defense: Winawer Variation
learningOutcomes: **Play** the Winawer through move 10.
**Explain** the pin on c3 and the pawn structure after ...dxc4.
**Value** complexity — understanding that the most complex positions reward the most study.
lessons.inquiryQuestion: How does Black's bishop pin turn the French into a razor-sharp battle — and why is the Winawer feared by White players?

lessons.title: French Defense: Classical and Tarrasch
learningOutcomes: **Play** the Classical French and Tarrasch through move 10.
**Explain** the blocked center and the ...c5/...f6 pawn breaks.
**Value** resilience — understanding that cramped positions can become powerful if survived.
lessons.inquiryQuestion: How does the French Defense's cramped position turn into a dangerous counter-attack — and why do players love suffering?

lessons.title: The Caro-Kann Defense
learningOutcomes: **Play** the Caro-Kann main line through move 8.
**Explain** the ...d5 break and the light-squared bishop development.
**Value** reliability — understanding that solid openings build confidence.
lessons.inquiryQuestion: Why is the Caro-Kann called the 'easy French' — and what makes it the most reliable defense for beginners?

lessons.title: The Pirc Defense
learningOutcomes: **Play** the Pirc through move 8.
**Explain** the hypermodern idea of inviting White forward then countering.
**Value** counter-punching — understanding that letting the opponent overextend is a strategy.
lessons.inquiryQuestion: How does the Pirc invite White to build a big center — and why is that exactly what Black wants?

lessons.title: The Modern Defense
learningOutcomes: **Play** the Modern through move 8.
**Explain** the ...Bg7/...d6 setup and the ...c5/...d5 breaks.
**Value** flexibility — understanding that delaying the center fight creates options.
lessons.inquiryQuestion: How does 1...g6 flip opening theory on its head — and when is delaying the center fight better than joining it?

lessons.title: Alekhine's Defense
learningOutcomes: **Play** the Alekhine through move 8.
**Explain** the provocative idea of attacking the e4 pawn from the start.
**Value** audacity — understanding that challenging conventions can be brilliant.
lessons.inquiryQuestion: How does attacking White's center on move 1 create one of chess's most provocative defenses — and is it genius or madness?

lessons.title: The Scandinavian Defense
learningOutcomes: **Play** the Scandinavian through move 6.
**Explain** why bringing the queen out early is usually bad — and why it works here.
**Value** simplicity — understanding that the easiest openings to learn can still be effective.
